paragraphs: Classifying a time series becomes difficult when measurements are sparse and arrive at uneven intervals. The gaps create uncertainty about the underlying process, and different observation schedules do not naturally fit classifiers that expect inputs with a fixed number of features. This paper develops a framework that addresses both issues together.

Its central component is a Gaussian process adapter: a computational layer connecting irregular observations to a classifier while accounting for uncertainty about the temporal process. The framework can work with any black-box classifier that can be learned through gradient descent. This makes the adapter a general interface between the observation format and the prediction model.

The authors combine structured kernel interpolation with the Lanczos approximation method to make the required computations scalable. They also show how backpropagation can train the adapter and classifier jointly. Consequently, the adapter can be adjusted for the classification objective as part of the complete system, bringing uncertainty-aware processing into an end-to-end learning framework.
neurips-2016-a-scalable-end-to-end-gauss.tldr: A scalable Gaussian process adapter connects sparse, irregular time series to gradient-trained classifiers while accounting for uncertainty.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems in which one expected-value function is applied to the output of another. Such an objective has two connected layers of averaging, so learning from samples must account for the composition as well as the randomness. The authors propose accelerated stochastic compositional proximal gradient, or ASC-PG, for this setting.

ASC-PG is a first-order method that obtains information from a sampling oracle and updates on two different timescales. It also accommodates nonsmooth regularization penalties. The abstract identifies it as the first proximal gradient method for stochastic composition with this capability, extending the kinds of objectives that this optimization approach can handle.

The theoretical results establish faster convergence than the previously best-known algorithms and optimal sample-error complexity in several important special cases. Optimality is therefore a result for those cases, rather than a claim about every composition problem. The authors also apply the method to reinforcement learning and conduct numerical experiments, connecting the optimization framework to a concrete learning application.
neurips-2016-accelerating-stochastic-com.tldr: ASC-PG accelerates stochastic composition optimization, supports nonsmooth penalties, and achieves optimal sample-error complexity in several special cases.

paragraphs: A reusable skill in reinforcement learning is an action that unfolds over time, also called an option. Learning such a skill leaves another question: in which situations should the agent use it? Adaptive Skills, Adaptive Partitions, or ASAP, learns both the skills and where they apply within a single framework.

This separation gives the agent a way to approach related new tasks by changing where it uses skills it already possesses. The learned behavior can remain useful even when the appropriate circumstances for applying it change. The authors view this combination of skill learning and application learning as a building block for agents that continue learning across tasks.

The paper proves convergence to a local optimum under conditions described as natural, so the guarantee does not establish a globally best solution. Experiments, including a RoboCup domain, show that ASAP learns where to reuse skills and solves multiple tasks with considerably less experience than learning each task from scratch. These findings support its proposed role in sharing learned behavior across related tasks.
neurips-2016-adaptive-skills-adaptive-pa.tldr: ASAP jointly learns reusable skills and where to apply them, reducing the experience needed across tasks in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much easier clustering becomes when a learner can consult a domain expert. The permitted question is simple: do these two instances belong to the same cluster? The proposed semi-supervised active clustering framework studies both the number of expert questions and the computation required to produce a clustering.

The analysis assumes that the expert follows a center-based clustering with a specified margin condition. For the k-means case, the authors give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm using O(k² log k + k log n) queries and O(kn log n) time, where k counts clusters and n counts instances. Its success guarantee depends on the stated margin condition.

The striking comparison is that clustering remains NP-hard without queries even under that margin condition. A relatively small amount of expert interaction can therefore make an otherwise computationally hard problem efficiently solvable in this setting. A lower bound on the required queries also shows that expert input has a quantifiable computational value, rather than being an unrestricted source of help.
neurips-2016-clustering-with-same-cluste.tldr: Under a margin condition, a small number of same-cluster queries enables efficient clustering where computation alone remains NP-hard.

paragraphs: Decision makers can make different kinds of mistakes, and those patterns can change over time. Confusions over Time, or CoT, is a Bayesian generative framework for describing both individual error patterns and broader trends across a collection of decision makers. Its goal includes making those patterns interpretable.

The model represents errors through time-dependent confusion matrices, which describe how decisions confuse one category with another as time passes. It groups similar decision makers and judged items into clusters. Each cluster receives a representative prototype and a feature indicator identifying the attributes most important to characterizing that group.

Together, these components connect individual behavior with collective patterns at multiple levels of detail. The prototype describes a representative member, while the selected features explain what distinguishes the cluster. Experiments use real-world data involving bail decisions, asthma treatments, and insurance policy approvals. The reported results show that CoT can accurately model and explain changing confusion patterns in those settings, supporting the framework's combination of temporal modeling and interpretable grouping.
neurips-2016-confusions-over-time-an-int.tldr: CoT models changing decision errors with time-dependent confusion matrices and explains collective patterns through interpretable clusters.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering uses recorded preferences to recommend new items, but accepted recommendations then influence the records used for future predictions. The resulting feedback loop mixes users' intrinsic preferences with the recommender's own influence. This paper investigates whether that influence can be identified and separated from a user-item rating matrix.

The authors state sufficient assumptions under which reversing the feedback process remains computationally tractable. They also develop a metric for measuring the recommender's influence across the rating matrix. This provides a way to investigate how much the observed data reflect the system that helped generate them.

On synthetic and real-world datasets, the metric is used to assess overall influence, rank frequently recommended items, and distinguish recommended ratings from intrinsic preferences. The results indicate that recovering an intrinsic-preference rating matrix may be possible from a single snapshot, without temporal records. This is a qualified recovery finding within the proposed framework and assumptions, rather than a guarantee that every observed rating matrix can be uniquely disentangled.
neurips-2016-deconvolving-feedback-loops.tldr: Under sufficient assumptions, recommender feedback can be disentangled, with results suggesting intrinsic preferences can be recovered from one rating-matrix snapshot.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization analyzes data organized along multiple dimensions. Nonlinear versions can capture complex relationships, but existing approaches can be expensive and develop substantial learning bias when observations are extremely sparse. This paper proposes a flexible nonlinear model designed to support efficient distributed inference and more freedom in selecting training observations.

The model avoids the costly Kronecker-product computations and structural restrictions found in existing tensor Gaussian process formulations. In particular, it allows an arbitrary subset of tensor entries to be used for training. The authors derive a tractable, tight variational evidence lower bound, an optimization objective that enables approximate inference while separating much of the computation.

That separation supports a distributed inference algorithm within MapReduce. The algorithm avoids key-value operations and can exploit memory caching in systems such as Spark. Experiments report advantages over several state-of-the-art approaches in both prediction and computational efficiency. The contribution connects modeling flexibility with an inference objective and execution strategy intended to make that flexibility practical at scale.
neurips-2016-distributed-flexible-nonlin.tldr: A flexible nonlinear tensor model enables arbitrary training subsets and distributed inference, improving prediction and efficiency in experiments.

paragraphs: Solving a least-squares problem on a large dataset can be expensive, so sampling a smaller collection of observations is a useful shortcut. The paper questions sampling rules that consider the input features but ignore the response values. Responses also carry information relevant to deciding which observations should receive attention.

The proposed gradient-based sampling method uses both inputs and outputs by assigning sampling probabilities according to data points' gradient values. Computing those probabilities takes O(nd) time, where n is the full number of observations and d is the input dimension. This matters because the preparation needed to choose a sample is itself part of the computational cost.

The authors analyze error for general importance sampling relative to the least-squares solution obtained from the complete dataset. Their analysis establishes improved performance from the proposed gradient-based choice. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets also support advantages over existing sampling approaches in statistical efficiency and computational savings. The method therefore ties the selection of observations directly to information relevant to the fitting problem.
neurips-2016-gradient-based-sampling-an-.tldr: Gradient-based sampling uses inputs and responses to select observations for faster, statistically efficient least-squares fitting.

paragraphs: Measurements from different sources can differ because their underlying populations differ or because the measurement processes distort them differently. This paper studies how to test whether two underlying distributions are equal when only transformed samples are observed. The transformations belong to known function classes, providing structure for separating measurement effects from distributional differences.

The authors build a hypothesis-testing framework that estimates the distortions together with the statistical test. This joint treatment addresses a problem arising when clinical and imaging biomarkers are combined across sites or batches. Such distortions can obstruct analyses that would otherwise benefit from larger pooled samples.

The paper develops a simple algorithm, examines its convergence and consistency, and supplies lower-bound strategies using ideas from continuous optimization. On data from individuals at risk for neurological disease, the reported results are competitive with alternative procedures that cost twice as much and can be operationally infeasible. The contribution concerns comparing distributions despite measurement transformations, with the biomedical application illustrating why this distinction matters.
neurips-2016-hypothesis-testing-in-unsup.tldr: A joint testing-and-distortion-estimation framework compares underlying distributions using transformed measurements from different sources.

paragraphs: A graphical model can be used to produce several plausible labelings while encouraging those answers to differ. This paper studies jointly finding M such labelings for binary submodular energies, including higher-order interactions. Its central insight connects this diversity objective to a family of submodular optimization problems controlled by one parameter.

The connection relies on a shared nested structure in the solutions. For certain diversity measures, the desired labelings can be recovered by solving M ordinary submodular minimization problems at different parameter values. Those values have closed-form expressions that can be computed before optimization begins, allowing the individual problems to run in parallel. In a special case, the required solver is max-flow.

The theory leads to two algorithms that the authors report outperform competitors in runtime and result quality. In particular, they compute exact jointly diverse labelings faster than a popular approach that yields approximate solutions in the sense discussed by the paper. The result makes a structured diversity objective accessible through existing optimization machinery under the specified conditions.
neurips-2016-joint-m-best-diverse-labeli.tldr: For certain diversity measures, exact jointly diverse labelings reduce to independent submodular optimizations with parameters computed in advance.

paragraphs: This paper considers a continuous phenomenon that changes across space and time, while only a few sensor measurements are available. The goal is to infer its hidden state. The authors combine a kernel representation of the spatial function with a dynamical systems prior governing how the model's weights evolve over time.

This construction provides a valid approach to spatiotemporal modeling without necessarily requiring the design of complicated nonstationary kernels. Temporal structure enters through the evolving weights. The predictive model also informs where measurements should be taken, connecting the representation of the phenomenon with the design of the sensing process.

The authors give sufficient conditions on both the number and spatial placement of samples that guarantee recovery of the hidden state. They also establish a lower bound on the measurements needed for robust inference. These results distinguish arrangements that suffice for recovery from a fundamental requirement on sample count. Numerical experiments show the approach outperforming existing methods, supporting the combined use of dynamical modeling and carefully chosen sensing locations.
neurips-2016-kernel-observers-systems-th.tldr: Kernel observers combine evolving model weights with sensor placement theory to recover spatiotemporal hidden states from few measurements.

paragraphs: Clustering guided by a user aims to recover groups that match the user's perception. Traditional guidance often concerns particular examples, such as seed assignments or constraints on pairs. If those examples are selected nonrandomly, their sampling bias can steer the algorithm toward groups that fail to reflect the intended organization.

This paper proposes adding supervision at the feature level. It represents such guidance through perception vectors, which the authors say can be obtained easily in many applications. Their Perception Embedded clustering algorithms use these vectors together with traditional side information to find groups aligned with the user's view.

The approach changes how the user's intended grouping is communicated: guidance can describe relevant features as well as relationships among selected instances. This directly addresses the concern that instance-level supervision may offer a biased picture of the desired clusters. Extensive experiments on real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Perception Embedded clustering empirically. Those results support feature-level supervision as a useful source of guidance, without establishing that sampling bias is eliminated in every application.
neurips-2016-learning-user-perceived-clu.tldr: Perception Embedded clustering combines feature-level perception vectors with traditional supervision to better recover user-perceived groups.

paragraphs: A neural network can classify ordinary inputs accurately yet change its answer after a small adversarial perturbation. This paper develops metrics for measuring that vulnerability and an algorithm for approximating the metrics. Its approach represents robustness through a linear program, turning the assessment into a constrained optimization problem.

Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 show how the metrics can evaluate deep networks. The authors report that their algorithm produces more informative robustness estimates than estimates obtained using existing algorithms. The emphasis is on measuring sensitivity in a way that reveals more about the model than its ordinary classification accuracy does.

The paper also finds that existing robustness-improvement approaches can overfit to adversarial examples produced by a particular generation algorithm. That finding makes the evaluation procedure consequential: success against one source of adversarial inputs may reflect specialization to that source. The authors further show that their techniques can improve robustness under both their newly proposed metrics and previously proposed ones, linking assessment with model improvement.
neurips-2016-measuring-neural-net-robust.tldr: Constraint-based robustness estimates reveal adversarial-training overfitting and help improve neural networks under new and existing robustness metrics.

paragraphs: Visual question answering requires a model to combine information from an image with information from a question. This paper introduces Multimodal Residual Networks, or MRN, to extend residual learning to that joint task. The aim is to learn a representation in which visual and language information interact within the network.

The key operation is element-wise multiplication in the joint residual mappings. This combines corresponding components of the two information sources and draws on residual learning in attentional models. The authors also explore alternative model designs arising from the multimodal setting, investigating how the two sources can be brought together.

MRN achieves the reported state-of-the-art results on the Visual QA dataset for both open-ended answers and multiple-choice questions. The paper additionally introduces a backpropagation-based method for visualizing the attention effect of each learning block's joint representation. This visualization works even though the visual features have been collapsed without retaining spatial information, providing a way to inspect how the learned multimodal representations relate to attention.
neurips-2016-multimodal-residual-learnin.tldr: MRN combines image and language features through multiplicative residual mappings, achieving leading reported Visual QA results and enabling attention visualization.

paragraphs: Rademacher observations, or rados, are class-related sufficient statistics that can support learning linear classifiers. Earlier work established separate equivalences between learning from examples and learning from rados for logistic and square losses. This paper develops a common theory that unifies and generalizes those previously separate results.

The theory also exposes a connection to regularization. Under a sufficient condition, regularizing the example-based loss is equivalent to modifying the rados used in the corresponding rado loss. This moves the regularization effect into the transformed data and suggests that an efficient learning routine may remain efficient when the regularizer changes.

The authors provide a boosting algorithm for regularized exponential rado loss using one master routine across ridge, lasso, SLOPE, infinity-norm, and elastic-net regularization. Because this rado loss corresponds to regularized logistic loss over examples, the algorithm supplies an efficient proxy across that range of penalties. Experiments show that regularization substantially improves rado-based learning and compares favorably with example-based learning, supporting the practical value of the theoretical connection.
neurips-2016-on-regularizing-rademacher-.tldr: A unified theory connects example and rado losses, enabling one boosting routine to handle a broad range of regularizers.

paragraphs: Non-negative matrix factorization decomposes data into feature and weight matrices whose entries cannot be negative. Although it works well in practice, recovering the underlying factors requires theoretical justification. This paper proposes an alternating algorithm that repeatedly decodes weights and updates features, then analyzes when it recovers the true factors.

The recovery guarantee assumes a generative model and conditions described as fairly mild. The essential requirement on the features is linear independence. The algorithm uses ReLU when decoding weights to exploit their non-negativity, making that structural constraint an active part of how the hidden components are recovered.

The analysis establishes tolerance to adversarial noise that can potentially reach the scale of the signal, as well as unbiased noise much larger than the signal. These are qualified robustness statements within the recovery framework. The proof couples two carefully designed potential functions to track the algorithm's progress. Together, the algorithm and analysis connect a practically successful alternating procedure with conditions for recovering meaningful ground-truth components despite substantial noise.
neurips-2016-recovery-guarantee-of-non-n.tldr: An alternating non-negative factorization algorithm provably recovers ground-truth factors under a generative model and tolerates substantial noise.

paragraphs: An encoder-decoder model turns an input into internal representations and then generates an output sequence. This paper inserts a review stage between those operations. The review network revisits the encoder's hidden states through attention, producing a sequence of intermediate representations before the decoder uses them to generate a caption.

Each review step produces what the authors call a thought vector. The decoder's attention mechanism then operates on these vectors. This creates a way to process the encoded information further before generation, with several review steps supplying the representations on which the decoder focuses. The paper considers recurrent decoders paired with both convolutional and recurrent encoders.

The framework is presented as a general extension capable of enhancing existing encoder-decoder models, and conventional encoder-decoders are shown to be a special case. Empirically, review networks improve on state-of-the-art encoder-decoder systems for image captioning and source code captioning. The two applications support the usefulness of the review stage across different input types within the tested generation tasks.
neurips-2016-review-networks-for-caption.tldr: Review networks add attentive processing between encoding and decoding, improving image and source code captioning in experiments.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems place their solutions on curved spaces called Riemannian manifolds. This paper studies objectives that are finite sums of functions smooth along the geometry of such a space. It introduces Riemannian SVRG, extending stochastic variance reduction beyond the vector-space setting addressed by existing work.

The authors analyze both geodesically convex objectives and smooth nonconvex objectives. Their results show that the method retains advantages of ordinary SVRG, while the manifold's curvature contributes factors that affect convergence. Geometry therefore enters the performance guarantees explicitly, rather than merely changing how an update is represented.

The paper presents the method as the first provably fast stochastic Riemannian approach to the authors' knowledge. It also supplies a non-asymptotic complexity analysis for nonconvex Riemannian optimization, described as new even for batch methods. Such an analysis addresses finite computational effort. One implication is a geometric perspective on variance-reduced principal component analysis, which the authors suggest could yield a short and transparent convergence argument.
neurips-2016-riemannian-svrg-fast-stocha.tldr: Riemannian SVRG extends variance reduction to curved spaces with convergence guarantees that explicitly depend on manifold curvature.

paragraphs: Exploration can be unacceptable when a single unsafe action risks failure or environmental harm. This paper studies exploration in finite Markov decision processes with an initially unknown safety constraint depending on states and actions. The constraint has regularity properties represented through a Gaussian process prior.

The proposed SAFEMDP algorithm gathers noisy observations while cautiously visiting safe states and taking safe actions. It uses those observations to build statistical confidence about state-action pairs it has not visited. It also considers reachability explicitly, including whether a state has a safe way out, so exploration does not trap the agent.

Under the stated safety framework and regularity conditions, the authors prove that SAFEMDP completely explores the safely reachable portion of the process without breaking the constraint. The scope is the safely reachable region, with the guarantee relying on the modeling assumptions. A rover exploring an unknown map represented by digital terrain models demonstrates the approach, linking uncertainty about local safety with the need to preserve safe movement through the environment.
neurips-2016-safe-exploration-in-finite-.tldr: Under its regularity assumptions, SAFEMDP explores the safely reachable region while learning unknown constraints and preserving safe escape routes.

paragraphs: When data are limited, replacing an established decision strategy with a learned one can reduce performance. This paper defines a safe policy as one guaranteed to perform at least as well as a baseline. It studies how to pursue that goal using an inaccurate dynamics model whose accuracy guarantees are known.

The proposed robust formulation directly optimizes performance relative to the baseline through a regret objective. This allows improvement in states where the dynamics are accurately modeled while falling back to the baseline elsewhere. The baseline therefore guides how the method responds to uneven knowledge about the system.

The authors show that their formulation is NP-hard and develop an approximate algorithm to make the approach usable. Experiments across several domains show that even this relatively simple approximation can substantially outperform standard approaches. The theoretical formulation and empirical approximation serve distinct roles: the formulation captures robust baseline-relative improvement, while the experiments demonstrate the practical promise of the proposed approximation under model uncertainty.
neurips-2016-safe-policy-improvement-by-.tldr: Robust baseline-regret optimization targets policy improvements where dynamics are accurate and fallback behavior where they are uncertain.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning when an algorithm can inspect only a limited number of attributes of each example. The restriction is formalized through the limited attribute observation model. The central question is how accurately regression or classification can be learned when access to each example's information is constrained.

The authors establish lower bounds on attainable precision for several learning problems. These include linear regression with absolute loss or squared loss, and classification with hinge loss. Because the bounds apply to any algorithm in the relevant setting, they identify limits imposed by restricted observations rather than shortcomings of a particular training procedure.

The paper complements those impossibility results with a general-purpose algorithm that provides an upper bound on the achievable precision limit. The two sides describe both a barrier that algorithms cannot overcome and a level of performance an algorithm can attain. Together, they give a theoretical account of the consequences of missing attributes across several loss functions, without asserting that the upper and lower bounds coincide.
neurips-2016-the-limits-of-learning-with.tldr: The paper bounds achievable learning precision when only a limited number of attributes per example can be observed.

paragraphs: The paper examines a search problem involving an unlimited supply of coins of two types. Heavy coins have a higher probability of heads, but they are less common. The learner wants to identify a heavy coin using few flips, balancing inspection of new coins against further testing of already selected ones.

Neither type's probability of heads nor the proportion of heavy coins is known. This creates an ambiguity: difficulty finding a heavy coin could mean that heavy coins are rare or that the two types behave very similarly. The authors propose an adaptive algorithm that needs no prior knowledge of those parameters and still achieves near-optimal sample complexity.

A lower bound shows that non-adaptive strategies require at least quadratically more samples in the studied setting. The result quantifies the value of adjusting exploration as observations arrive. The paper also connects the problem to anomaly detection and establishes sample-complexity lower bounds for distinguishing one parametric distribution from a mixture of two, extending the breadth-versus-depth question to statistical testing.
neurips-2016-the-power-of-adaptivity-in-.tldr: An adaptive heavy-coin search needs no parameter knowledge and achieves near-optimal sampling, while non-adaptive strategies face a quadratic disadvantage.

paragraphs: Drift-diffusion models describe decisions as noisy evidence accumulating until a threshold is reached. This paper asks how an animal might learn that threshold. The authors construct trial-level rewards whose average across many trials matches Wald's cost function, linking a learnable reward signal to a criterion for optimal decisions.

Individual rewards are highly stochastic, making optimization challenging. The paper explores two approaches: a simple two-factor reward-modulated rule derived from REINFORCE, and Bayesian optimization using a Gaussian process. Both address threshold learning through the constructed reward function, but they differ in how efficiently they use trials and computation.

Bayesian optimization converges using fewer trials, yet requires more computation and exhibits greater variance. REINFORCE better matches animal acquisition behavior, and a similar learning rule has been proposed in models of basal ganglia function. The findings therefore distinguish efficiency measured in experience from computational efficiency and behavioral fit. They provide two ways to learn thresholds while identifying why the simpler rule may be a more suitable account of observed learning.
neurips-2016-threshold-learning-for-opti.tldr: Two reward-based methods learn decision thresholds, with Bayesian optimization using fewer trials and REINFORCE better matching animal learning behavior.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient Monte Carlo methods make posterior inference practical on large datasets by computing gradients from small subsets of observations. This reduces the cost of an update, but the resulting gradients can have high variance. In stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, that variability can impair performance and slow movement through the target distribution.

The paper introduces variance-reduction techniques for these gradient estimates, yielding new stochastic Monte Carlo methods. The objective is to retain the computational benefits of using subsets while reducing the variability that undermines sampling. This addresses the quality of the information driving each update, which directly influences the method's convergence behavior.

The authors establish better theoretical convergence-rate guarantees than stochastic Langevin dynamics. They also report strong empirical results on real-world datasets spanning regression, classification, independent component analysis, and mixture modeling. These findings supply both analytical and experimental support for variance reduction in stochastic sampling. The range of tested tasks shows its usefulness across several inference problems, while the theoretical result specifically concerns improved convergence guarantees.
neurips-2016-variance-reduction-in-stoch.tldr: Reducing stochastic-gradient variance improves Langevin sampling's theoretical convergence guarantees and empirical performance across four learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies probabilistic models over binary variables with a mixture of log-submodular and log-supermodular higher-order potentials. These components allow interactions among groups of variables. Together, they can represent arbitrary binary distributions, making the model family broader than pairwise Markov random fields or models restricted to log-supermodular potentials.

That expressive power makes inference difficult: the general problem is #P-hard. The authors develop efficient approximate inference algorithms using advances in discrete optimization. The approach seeks to make reasoning with this richer model family practical through approximation, while retaining its ability to describe varied interactions.

The experiments focus on preferences over sets of items that can include both complements and substitutes. Complements capture items whose joint presence is attractive, while substitutes capture alternatives within a selection. A model that supports both can express different relationships within the same preference problem. A large collection of experiments demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed approach, supporting the use of mixed potentials when preferences depend on how items combine.
neurips-2016-variational-inference-in-mi.tldr: Discrete-optimization-based approximate inference makes expressive binary models with both complementary and substitutable item relationships practical.
